A truce is a mutual, temporary agreement between two opposing sides to stop fighting each other. Both sides agree — at the same time — to pause their conflict for a set period or until a certain condition is met. Neither side wins, neither side surrenders. They simply agree to stop, together, for a while.

Think of it like pressing a "pause button" on a fight — one that both players press at the same time.
Breaking It Down — Three Key Parts

Every truce has three essential qualities. Miss any one of them, and it's not really a truce:

1. It is mutual.
One side alone cannot declare a truce. Both (or all) opposing sides must agree to it. If only one side stops fighting while the other keeps going, that's a surrender or a retreat — not a truce. A truce is always a two-way street.

2. It is temporary.
This is the most important thing to understand about a truce. It is not a permanent end to the conflict. It is a pause — a breathing space. The underlying disagreement or hostility is still there; the two sides have simply agreed not to act on it for now. The fight could resume when the truce ends.

3. It is specific.
A truce usually has a defined purpose or timeframe. It might last for a few hours, a few days, or even years. It is often called for a specific reason — to allow the wounded to be rescued, to let negotiations happen, to observe a religious holiday, or simply to prevent further bloodshed while a longer solution is worked out.

In War and Military Conflict

This is the most classic use of the word. When two armies or two countries are at war and they agree to stop shooting at each other temporarily, that agreement is called a truce.

After weeks of heavy fighting, the two armies agreed to a truce to recover their dead and tend to the wounded.

A famous real-world example is the Christmas Truce of 1914, during World War I, when German and British soldiers spontaneously stopped fighting on Christmas Eve and even played football together in No Man's Land — before the war resumed.

In Politics

The word is used when political rivals or opposing groups agree to stop attacking, criticizing, or undermining each other — at least for a while.

The two political parties declared a truce during the national crisis and agreed to work together.

In Everyday Personal Life

You don't need a war to use this word. In everyday language, a truce is used whenever two people who are arguing or feuding agree to stop — even temporarily.

After days of arguing, the two brothers finally called a truce.
"Truce?" she asked, extending her hand. He shook it. The argument was over — for now.

This informal use is extremely common and completely natural.

Understanding what a truce is not helps sharpen your understanding of what it is:

A truce is not peace.
Peace is a permanent, resolved end to conflict. A truce is temporary. After a truce, a war can — and often does — resume. Peace means the conflict is over. A truce only means the conflict is on hold.

A truce is not a surrender.
When someone surrenders, they admit defeat and submit to the other side. A truce involves no defeat and no submission. Both sides remain equal in status — they have simply chosen to stop fighting for now.

A truce is not a peace treaty.
A peace treaty is a formal, legal, and typically permanent document that ends a conflict and sets terms for the future. A truce is informal by comparison — it is simply a mutual agreement to pause. A peace treaty often follows a truce, but they are not the same thing.
Common Ways This Word Is Used in Sentences

These phrases come up constantly with the word truce:

  • Call a truce — to mutually decide to stop fighting → "Let's call a truce."
  • Declare a truce — to formally announce a stop to fighting
  • Agree to a truce — to accept a pause in conflict
  • Break a truce — to violate the agreement and start fighting again → "He broke the truce by attacking at dawn."
  • Negotiate a truce — to work out the terms of a temporary stop to fighting
  • Reach a truce — to successfully arrive at a mutual agreement to stop
  • Honor a truce — to respect and uphold the agreement
  • An uneasy truce — a truce that feels unstable or fragile, where both sides are suspicious of each other
  • A fragile truce — similar; a truce that could easily break down
The Tone and Feel of the Word

The word "truce" carries a feeling of tension held in check. When you read or hear that two sides have agreed to a truce, you understand that things were bad, that both sides are exhausted or cautious, and that the situation is still unresolved. A truce is not a happy ending — it is more like a cautious pause before the story continues.

It can also carry a feeling of relief — especially in personal contexts. When two friends call a truce after a long argument, there is a sense of both sides being ready to let go of the hostility, even if the issue isn't fully settled.
One Sentence to Remember It By

If you had to remember just one thing about this word, let it be this:

A truce is a temporary, mutual agreement to stop fighting — not because the conflict is over, but because both sides have chosen to pause it.

That single idea captures everything essential about the word truce.
